channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: AI-powered cognitive remediation for schizophrenia: a psychologist's lens on evidence and scalability in India
item.description: A PRISMA guided umbrella review pulls together 48 studies on AI assisted cognitive remediation for schizophrenia spectrum disorders, reading the evidence specifically through what is deliverable in India and comparable low and middle income settings. Reported effects run from moderate to large, with virtual reality social cognition training showing the largest benefits and smartphone delivered programmes doing well on working memory and engagement. The finding that matters operationally is that hybrid and clinician monitored formats retain people better than fully self directed ones, which cuts against the usual scalability pitch for autonomous tools. The authors are candid that the evidence base is heterogeneous and leans on small pilots and mixed quality reviews, and they frame the workforce gap, 0.75 psychiatrists per 100,000 people, as the real constraint these tools would have to relieve.

item.title: MedPRESS: a multi-turn benchmark for patient-pressure-induced medical sycophancy in LLMs
item.description: MedPRESS tests whether models hold on to correct medical guidance when a patient pushes back, using 600 medically grounded five turn dialogues across medication demands, personal self care, and symptom triage, where each exchange escalates through personal experience, social proof, claimed external evidence, and finally direct challenge. Across 20 models spanning general, medical, lightweight, large, open weight and proprietary families, models frequently drift into unsafe agreement under sustained pressure, with wide variation by family, scale and prompt type. Anti sycophancy prompting improves robustness for several models but does not eliminate the failure. The framing is directly relevant to this feed, since safe medical knowledge is not the same as safe medical behaviour, and static single question benchmarks cannot tell the two apart.

item.title: Persona-grounded safety evaluation of AI companions in multi-turn conversations
item.description: Rather than relying on self report or interviews, this framework simulates the users most likely to be harmed and then scores what a real companion app says back to them. Nine personas covering depression, anxiety, PTSD, eating disorders and incel identity were built with clinical and psychometric validation, then run through 25 high risk scenarios producing 1,674 dialogue pairs against Replika. The app shows a narrow emotional range dominated by curiosity and care, and frequently mirrors or normalises unsafe content including self harm, disordered eating and violent fantasy narratives. The contribution is methodological as much as empirical, supplying a reproducible testbed for auditing companion apps against specific psychiatric vulnerabilities rather than against a general population baseline.

item.title: A conditional companion: lived experiences of people with mental health disorders using LLMs
item.description: Interviews with UK adults who have mental health diagnoses trace why they reach for general purpose LLMs, and the reasons are structural rather than enthusiastic: immediacy and instant access, a non judgmental outlet for disclosure, the ability to disclose at their own pace, and help making sense of their own thinking. Participants drew consistent boundaries in the same three places, crisis and emergency, socially and emotionally complex situations, and relational depth, which is where they judged the tool to stop being adequate. The authors read this as conditional rather than wholesale adoption, with people actively managing what they share and how far they let an exchange go. The design implications point toward supporting that boundary setting rather than smoothing it away in the name of engagement.

item.title: SocialWise: LLM-agentic conversation therapy for individuals with autism spectrum disorder
item.description: SocialWise is a browser based conversation therapy prototype pairing LLM role play agents with a retrieval grounded knowledge base of autism therapy documents, letting a user pick a scenario, practise by text or voice, and receive structured feedback on tone, engagement and alternative phrasing. A remote pilot with 34 autistic adults reported helpfulness of 4.15 out of 5 with unanimous willingness to recommend, and the most cited gains were turn taking, problem solving in social conflict, and reduced anxiety during real conversations afterward. The stated motivation is access, since social skills training is bounded by cost, geography and provider availability. It is worth reading alongside the masking literature in this feed, because a tool that coaches toward smoother neurotypical phrasing is also, unavoidably, coaching toward passing.

item.title: Automating injustice: a critical analysis of AI-assisted recruitment processes from a disability justice perspective
item.description: This paper argues that AI assisted recruitment does not remove hiring bias so much as launder it, converting human judgment into data and thereby making the resulting discrimination harder to see and harder to contest. Reading the pipeline through disability justice, it treats classification itself as the harm, since disability becomes a penalising feature once it is rendered as a variable, and it links the underlying data practices to a broader pattern of extractive collection. Psychometric testing and facial analysis get specific attention as the mechanisms that penalise neurodivergent candidates and anyone whose embodiment departs from the norm a model has learned. The conclusion is that AI hiring tools reconfigure bias into more opaque and less accountable forms rather than eliminating it.

item.title: A pragmatic classification framework for AI incident monitoring
item.description: Public AI incident databases now hold thousands of records, but raw counts conflate three separate things: how likely an incident is to be reported at all, how widely the system is actually deployed, and how often harm occurs per unit of that exposure. This framework pulls them apart, pairing a structured monitoring question with a tiered estimation process that derives harm and exposure trends independently, then mapping the result onto governance categories of escalating, mitigating, concentrating, receding or unclassifiable. The authors are explicit that incident databases over represent acute, dramatic and Anglophone harms while under representing chronic and diffuse ones, which is precisely the failure mode for slowly accumulating psychiatric harm. That matters for this feed because adverse event reporting is the mechanism most chatbot safety proposals quietly depend on.

item.title: FTC seeks public comment on a policy statement addressing AI accuracy
item.description: The FTC has put out for comment a proposed policy statement treating undisclosed ideological tuning of AI outputs as potentially deceptive under Section 5 of the FTC Act, on the theory that consumers reasonably expect objectivity and accuracy from systems marketed for general use. The statement also asserts that state AI laws are impliedly preempted where they conflict with the federal scheme, naming Colorado's Artificial Intelligence Act as its example, which puts it in tension with the state level chatbot and mental health statutes tracked elsewhere in this feed. The comment window ran to 31 July 2026 and the authorising vote was 2 to 0. Nothing in the statement addresses disability, accessibility or clinical safety, so the accuracy it advances is a question about ideology rather than about harm to vulnerable users.
